appraisal_events.evidence: Robert's inherited Guermantes hauteur has 'stiffened' into something almost avian; entering a party he draws 'curiosité et l'admiration moitié mondaine, moitié zoologique,' but 'un rien d'indéfinissable' turns his Guermantes manner into M. de Charlus's; his tender speech to the narrator rings with 'une voix d'alcoolique et des modulations d'acteur.'
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's extended portrait admires Robert's exotic, birdlike allure even while showing it congeal into affectation and drift toward Charlus's manner, revealing performance and self-love beneath the glamour.

appraisal_events.evidence: Unlike the Courvoisiers, who accepted the vicomte's nature so that 'M. de Courvoisier n'en aima que plus sa femme' and the couple was 'cité comme le meilleur ménage de Paris,' Robert 'faisait mourir sa femme de jalousie en cherchant sans plaisir des maîtresses.'
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator sets Robert's conduct against the Courvoisiers' wiser, happier arrangement: where that family's acceptance produced a celebrated marriage, Robert's joyless, denial-driven pursuit of mistresses instead tortures his own wife with jealousy.

appraisal_events.evidence: Robert 'poursuivait son ancien bienfaiteur de sa haine,' repeating to Gilberte, in one form or another, what Morel had told him against Charlus.
appraisal_events.explanation: Robert relays Morel's disparaging talk about Charlus to Gilberte and pursues his former benefactor with open hatred, discrediting Charlus within the family's private conversation.

status_effects.explanation: The admiring bird imagery gives way to a sense of congealed affectation and imitation, closing with his slide toward Charlus's manner.
Unlike the Courvoisier marriage, held up by social report as Paris's best household, no such reputation attaches to the Saint-Loups; instead Robert's conduct visibly torments his wife.
Social report explicitly cites the Courvoisiers as 'le meilleur ménage de Paris,' a standing the passage sets in implicit contrast to the Saint-Loups.
As the wife made jealous by Robert's joyless pursuit of mistresses, she is the one who suffers within this comparison.
Robert repeats Morel's disparagement of Charlus and pursues his former benefactor with hatred, discrediting him within the family's private talk.

ambiguities: Gilberte's evasive, shifting answers about whether Albertine (and by extension Gilberte herself) was drawn to women are explicitly left uncertain by the narrator among several competing hypotheses; no appraisal event is assigned to that exchange because the passage itself withholds resolution.
